title: Posterolateral corner deficiency amplifies varus-related anterior cruciate ligament forces under dynamic loading: A biomechanical study.
authors: Gellhaus F, Deichsel A, Stening J, Albert A, Peez C, Behrendt P, Seekamp A, Raschke MJ, Horst K, Kittl C
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 19. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70654.
Online  ahead of print.

Posterolateral corner deficiency amplifies varus-related anterior cruciate 
ligament forces under dynamic loading: A biomechanical study.

Gellhaus F(1)(2), Deichsel A(3), Stening J(3), Albert A(3), Peez C(3), Behrendt 
P(2)(4), Seekamp A(1), Raschke MJ(3), Horst K(3), Kittl C(3).



PURPOSE: This study examined the influence of varus alignment, posterolateral 
corner (PLC) insufficiency, and PLC reconstruction on forces acting on the 
anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). It was hypothesized that increasing varus 
would increase ACL force, PLC transection would amplify this increase, and 
reconstruction would restore force toward PLC-intact values.
METHODS: Eight cadaveric knees (mean age 62 ± 12 years) underwent dynamic 
testing at 0°, 10°, 20°, 30° and 40° flexion under 200 N axial load in a 
materials testing machine with a custom five-degree-of-freedom setup. The ACL 
was tibially detached and refixated with 80 N using a custom tensioner. Lateral 
opening-wedge distal femoral osteotomy with external fixation and 
three-dimensionally printed wedges established 0°, 3°, 5° and 8° varus. Three 
conditions were tested: (1) native, (2) PLC transection (lateral collateral 
ligament and popliteus tendon) and (3) PLC reconstruction in Arciero technique.
RESULTS: Axial loading caused ACL forces in PLC-intact knees ranging from 
77.1 ± 7.3 N (neutral alignment in 20° flexion) to 109.9 ± 46.8 N (8° varus at 
40° flexion). Significant increases in ACL forces were observed at 30° 
(p = 0.006) and 40° (p = 0.001) of flexion with 8° varus. Following PLC 
transection, significant increases in ACL forces occurred at 5° varus and higher 
from 10° of flexion onwards, with a notable increase from 80.0 ± 12.3 (neutral) 
to 153.2 ± 58.4 N (8° varus, 40° flexion, p < 0.001). After PLC reconstruction, 
no significant effects of varus alignment or flexion on ACL forces were observed 
(p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Under axial compression and simulated varus-thrust loading 
conditions, varus alignment of 5° or less did not significantly increase ACL 
forces in PLC-intact knees, whereas 8° varus resulted in significantly increased 
ACL loading at selected flexion angles. PLC deficiency was associated with 
greater increases in ACL force with increasing varus alignment.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: NA.

title: Lateral extra-articular augmentation is associated with improved graft survival after revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Collazo C, Rivarola H, Palanconi M, Meninato M, Peñaherrera-Carrillo C, Barros Castro A, Endara Urresta F
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 19;21:101224. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101224. Online
ahead  of print.

Lateral extra-articular augmentation is associated with improved graft survival 
after revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Collazo C(1), Rivarola H(1), Palanconi M(1), Meninato M(1), Peñaherrera-Carrillo 
C(2), Barros Castro A(3), Endara Urresta F(4).



BACKGROUND: Revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains 
associated with higher graft failure rates and greater residual rotational 
laxity than primary reconstruction. Although lateral extra-articular 
augmentation has been increasingly incorporated into revision surgery, evidence 
remains limited by confounding related to treatment allocation.
PURPOSE: To evaluate the association between lateral extra-articular 
augmentation and graft survival after first-time single-stage revision ACLR 
using propensity score-based inverse probability of treatment-weighting (IPTW), 
and to compare postoperative rotational laxity and patient-reported outcomes, 
with the direct comparison between lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) and 
anterolateral ligament (ALL) reconstruction considered exploratory. We 
hypothesized that lateral extra-articular augmentation would be associated with 
lower graft-failure risk and less residual rotational laxity than isolated 
revision ACLR.
METHODS: A total of 364 consecutive patients undergoing first-time single-stage 
revision ACLR between January 2015 and December 2019 were screened at three 
high-volume knee centers. Sixty-four patients were excluded during eligibility 
assessment, leaving 300 eligible patients, all of whom were included in the 
final cohort. The observed treatment distribution was 100 isolated revision 
ACLRs, 100 revision ACLRs with LET, and 100 revision ACLRs with ALL 
reconstruction; these group sizes were not created by propensity-score matching, 
frequency matching, sampling, capping, or post hoc balancing. LET and ALL 
reconstruction were pooled as lateral extra-articular augmentation for the 
primary comparison. IPTW was used to improve balance in measured baseline 
characteristics. Secondary outcomes included residual pivot shift, instrumented 
anterior laxity, postoperative International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) 
and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) Sport scores, and return 
to preinjury sport.
RESULTS: During a mean follow-up of 5.8 ± 1.1 years, graft failure occurred in 
20 of 100 patients (20.0%) after isolated revision ACLR and 19 of 200 patients 
(9.5%) after lateral extra-articular augmentation. Five-year weighted graft 
survival was 79.9% after isolated revision and 90.6% after augmentation. Lateral 
augmentation was associated with a lower risk of graft failure (IPTW-adjusted 
hazard ratio [HR], 0.46; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.28-0.74; P = 0.002). 
Residual pivot shift was observed in 34 of 200 patients (17.0%) after 
augmentation and 34 of 100 patients (34.0%) after isolated revision ACLR 
(weighted odds ratio [OR], 0.42; 95% CI, 0.25-0.71; P = 0.001). Mean 
instrumented anterior laxity was 2.60 ± 1.00 mm after isolated revision ACLR and 
2.25 ± 0.85 mm after augmentation; the device-adjusted difference was -0.21 mm 
(95% CI, -0.38 to -0.04; P = 0.015) and was not considered clinically 
interpretable. Postoperative IKDC and KOOS Sport scores showed small 
between-group differences. The exploratory LET-versus-ALL comparison did not 
identify a significant difference in graft-failure risk (HR, 0.91; 95% CI, 
0.39-2.10; P = 0.82) and should not be interpreted as demonstrating equivalence.
CONCLUSION: In this propensity-weighted multicenter cohort, lateral 
extra-articular augmentation was associated with higher graft survival and less 
residual rotational laxity after first-time revision ACLR. The absolute 
difference in graft failure was 10.5 percentage points, whereas between-group 
differences in postoperative patient-reported outcomes and instrumented anterior 
laxity were small. The exploratory LET-versus-ALL comparison did not demonstrate 
equivalence. Because treatment allocation was nonrandomized and residual 
confounding may remain, the study demonstrates an association between lateral 
augmentation and lower graft-failure risk but cannot establish that augmentation 
itself caused the observed reduction in failures.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective multicenter comparative cohort 
study.

title: Concomitant Centralization Procedure With Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Repair May Have Zone-Specific Effects on the Medial Femoral Condyle and Enhance Repair Healing Compared With Isolated Root Repair: An In Vivo Experimental Study in Rabbit Knees.
authors: Dzidzishvili L, Nelson B, Santangelo K, Sikes KJ, Burton L, Del Águila López-Pintor Ó, Fernández-Valle ME, Goodrich L, Cole BJ, LaPrade RF, Chahla J
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 20:3635465261492230. doi: 10.1177/03635465261492230.
 Online ahead of print.

Concomitant Centralization Procedure With Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Repair 
May Have Zone-Specific Effects on the Medial Femoral Condyle and Enhance Repair 
Healing Compared With Isolated Root Repair: An In Vivo Experimental Study in 
Rabbit Knees.

Dzidzishvili L(1), Nelson B(2), Santangelo K(2), Sikes KJ(2), Burton L(2), Del 
Águila López-Pintor Ó(3), Fernández-Valle ME(3), Goodrich L(2), Cole BJ(4), 
LaPrade RF(5), Chahla J(4).



BACKGROUND: Short-term clinical outcomes of meniscal centralization are 
promising, but questions remain whether it can protect articular cartilage and 
delay osteoarthritis progression.
PURPOSE: To assess cartilage status and healing potential after isolated medial 
meniscus posterior root (MMPR) repair (RR) versus MMPR repair augmented with a 
centralization procedure (RR-CP) in a rabbit stifle model.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: MMPR tears were surgically induced in 16 New Zealand White rabbits. 
Eight underwent RR and 8 underwent RR-CP using interlocking knotless anchors; 
contralateral limbs served as controls. After 4 months, animals were euthanized 
and articular cartilage was harvested for macro- and microscopic evaluation, 
including repair tissue assessment for healing potential. Microscopic assessment 
was performed using the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) 
scoring system. Cartilage thickness and meniscal extrusion (ME) were assessed 
using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 9.4 T. The medial 
femoral condyle was divided into 3 regions of interest (anterior, central, and 
posterior), and zone-specific changes were evaluated.
RESULTS: The mean ± standard deviation gross pathology joint degeneration score 
was significantly higher in the RR group compared with the RR-CP group (12.3 ± 
2.2 vs 9.1 ± 2.0; P = .01). The mean OARSI score was significantly lower in the 
RR-CP group compared with the RR group (3.1 ± 1.6 vs 4.2 ± 1.5; P = .04). 
Nonhealed root repairs were more frequent in the RR group, and repair healing 
scores favored the RR-CP group (1.75 ± 0.5 vs 2.5 ± 0.7; P = .041). MRI 
demonstrated significantly reduced central and posterior cartilage thickness in 
the RR group compared with the RR-CP and control knees (P ≤ .02), with no 
difference anteriorly (P = .23). ME did not differ between the RR and RR-CP 
goups (P = .12). Both experimental groups showed greater chondral damage 
compared with contralateral controls (P < .001).
CONCLUSION: RR-CP was associated with reduced total joint cartilage damage and 
improved repair healing compared with isolated RR. MRI showed greater loss of 
central and posterior cartilage thickness after RR, while no difference in 
postoperative ME was detected. Both treatment groups demonstrated increased 
chondral damage compared with control knees.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study provides important biological insights into a 
clinically relevant question and establishes a foundation for future clinical 
investigations aimed at defining patient selection criteria and surgical 
indications for a concomitant meniscal centralization procedure.

DOI: 10.1177/03635465261492230
PMID: 42899379
ai_summary: Adding a 'centralization procedure' to standard medial meniscus posterior root repair in a rabbit model led to better healing and reduced cartilage damage compared to root repair alone.

title: Multicentric development and validation of a fully automated artificial intelligence system for planning medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy on weight-bearing anterior-posterior long leg radiographs: The ISAKOS John Joyce Award 2025.
authors: Rupp MC, von Schacky CE, Lindner FJ, Feucht MJ, Ehmann Y, Fritsch L, Doucas A, Haddadin S, Hinterwimmer F, Jung M, Russe MF, von Eisenhart-Rothe R, Siebenlist S, Wilhelm NJ
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 19. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70635.
Online  ahead of print.

Multicentric development and validation of a fully automated artificial 
intelligence system for planning medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy on 
weight-bearing anterior-posterior long leg radiographs: The ISAKOS John Joyce 
Award 2025.

Rupp MC(1), von Schacky CE(2), Lindner FJ(1), Feucht MJ(3), Ehmann Y(1), Fritsch 
L(1), Doucas A(1), Haddadin S(4), Hinterwimmer F(5), Jung M(6), Russe MF(6), von 
Eisenhart-Rothe R(5), Siebenlist S(1), Wilhelm NJ(4)(5).



PURPOSE: Preoperative planning, currently performed by orthopaedic surgeons 
(OS), is essential for successful osteotomy, but is labour-intensive and 
error-prone. As such, there is significant potential in the use of automated 
artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to augment the abilities of OS in 
managing lower extremity pathologies in a high-volume task that demands high 
precision and reliability. The aim was to develop a deep learning (DL) system 
capable of fully autonomous planning a medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy 
(mow-HTO) on weight bearing anterior posterior (AP) long leg radiographs (LLR) 
and to validate its agreement with an expert-derived reference standard, its 
reliability and processing time of the DL model compared to expert OS on 
multicentric test data sets (two institutions).
METHODS: A total of 594 patients (age 41.1 ± 13.2 years, 182 female) who 
underwent osteotomy between 01/2014 and 01/2021 were retrospectively enrolled. 
Manual annotations for lower extremity alignment and high tibial landmarks were 
performed on AP LLR radiographs. The data set was divided into training (60%, 
n = 399), validation (10%, n = 59) and hold-out testing (30%, n = 136), with an 
additional external dataset (n = 100) for further testing. A DL system with 
twelve expert networks was trained to identify relevant landmarks for HTO 
planning. The DL model was then tested on fully automated planning of a medial 
open wedge HTO based on (1) the desired postoperative intersection of the 
mechanical axis with the tibial plateau (%-based) and (2) the desired 
femorotibial axis (°-based). Agreement with the expert-derived reference, 
reliability and processing time were compared with three expert OS using 
FDA-approved preoperative planning software on the test data sets.
RESULTS: For preoperative alignment parameter analysis, compared to the ground 
truth, human preoperative accuracy ranged from 0.13° ± 0.10° to 1.06° ± 1.4°, 
interrater reliability ranged from intraclass correlation (ICC) 0.84-1.0 and 
clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 72% to 100%. Preoperative accuracy of 
the DL model ranged from 0.22° ± 0.18° to 1.04° ± 1.28°, interrater reliability 
ranged from ICC 0.93-1.0 and clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 91% to 
100%. For the planning of the osteotomy gap, compared to the ground truth, human 
accuracy ranged from 0.46 ± 0.65 mm to 0.5 ± 0.88 mm (%-based) and 0.43 ± 0.55 
to 0.52 ± 0.75 mm (°-based), reliability ranged from ICC 0.9-0.96 and 0.95-0.97 
and clinically acceptable accuracy was 93.6%-96.0% (%-based) and 89.8%-93.9% 
(°-based). For the DL model, the accuracy was 0.53 ± 0.63 mm (%-based) and 
0.44 ± 0.53 mm (°-based), reliability was ICC 0.99 (both methods) and clinically 
acceptable accuracy was 98.1% (%-based) and 96.2% (°-based). The DL-model 
significantly and substantially outperformed the OS in intrarater reliability 
(0.88 vs. 1.0) and processing time for a fully automated alignment analysis 
(25.3 ± 0.8 s vs. 148.7 ± 10.1 s, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The developed DL model enabled fully automated mow-HTO planning on 
AP long-leg radiographs with reliability comparable to that of expert OS while 
significantly reducing processing time and improving measurement consistency. 
These suggest that DL-based systems may assist orthopaedic providers by 
accelerating and standardising osteotomy planning.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.

Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy.

PMID: 42897441
ai_summary: An artificial intelligence system was developed that can plan high tibial osteotomies with accuracy and reliability comparable to expert surgeons, while significantly reducing the time required for planning.

title: Silk Dressings Are More Cost Effective Than 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh in Hip and Knee Arthroplasty.
authors: Aastroem KIM, Sarpong NO, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Long WJ, Shah RP
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 19. doi: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00591. Online
ahead  of print.

Silk Dressings Are More Cost Effective Than 2-Octyl Cyanoacrylate Mesh in Hip 
and Knee Arthroplasty.

Aastroem KIM(1), Sarpong NO, Neuwirth AL, Cooper HJ, Long WJ, Shah RP.



INTRODUCTION: Wound complications are costly after primary and revision total 
hip and knee arthroplasty (TJA). Mesh with 2-octyl cyanoacrylate can perform 
well but is associated with hypersensitivity and wound-healing complications. 
Silk dressings have shown fewer adverse events. We compared dressing costs, 
examining direct and complication-related expenses.
METHODS: An IRB-exempt cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted using published 
data on complication rates, including hypersensitivity reactions, delayed wound 
healing, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), and application times. Direct 
material costs were calculated and annualized using the manufacturer's suggested 
retail prices (MSRPs) and bulk-purchase rates. Indirect costs were calculated 
for surgical costs per minute and treatment of wound complications and PJI.
RESULTS: Direct material costs were $387 (MSRP) or $79 (bulk pricing) for mesh 
dressings versus $120 (MSRP) or $60 (bulk pricing) for silk. When application 
times, differential rates of sensitivity reactions, and wound complications and 
their management are applied to national TJA rates, mesh costs markedly more 
than silk by $939/patient (MSRP) and $690/patient (bulk pricing) (MSRP: $1,090 
versus $151/patient; $1.89 billion versus $2.62 million/annum; bulk pricing: 
$781 versus $91/patient; $1.36 billion versus $158 million/annum). Excluding 
PJI, which has a relationship that is several degrees away from dressing type, 
mesh was still more expensive than silk by $484/patient (MSRP) and $235/patient 
(bulk pricing) (MSRP: $634/patient versus $150; $1.1 billion versus $262 
million/annum; bulk pricing: $326/patient versus $91; $566 million vs. $158 
million/annum).
CONCLUSION: Silk dressings are more cost-effective than mesh dressings because 
of shorter application time, fewer complications, and lower pricing. For 
clinical and economic reasons, silk dressings should be considered for TJA.

behalf of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.

DOI: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-26-00591
PMID: 42895330
ai_summary: Silk dressings are more cost-effective than 2-octyl cyanoacrylate mesh for hip and knee replacements due to lower material costs, faster application times, and fewer wound-related complications.

title: A diagnostic model integrating clinical, magnetic resonance imaging, and arthroscopic findings accurately identified hypermobile lateral meniscus: Development and internal validation.
authors: Rivarola H, Collazo C, Palanconi M, Meninato M, Barros Castro A, Peñaherrera-Carrillo C, Endara Urresta F
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 19;21:101227. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101227. Online
ahead  of print.

A diagnostic model integrating clinical, magnetic resonance imaging, and 
arthroscopic findings accurately identified hypermobile lateral meniscus: 
Development and internal validation.

Rivarola H(1), Collazo C(1), Palanconi M(1), Meninato M(1), Barros Castro A(2), 
Peñaherrera-Carrillo C(3), Endara Urresta F(4).



BACKGROUND: To develop and internally validate a diagnostic model for 
hypermobile lateral meniscus (HLM) integrating clinical symptoms, magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) findings, and dynamic arthroscopic assessment.
METHODS: A retrospective diagnostic model study was performed, including 100 
consecutive patients evaluated for suspected lateral meniscal pathology at a 
tertiary knee surgery center. All patients underwent standardized clinical 
examination, preoperative MRI, and arthroscopic assessment of lateral meniscal 
mobility, which served as the reference standard. Candidate predictors were 
restricted to preoperative clinical and MRI variables, including intermittent 
locking, posterolateral McMurray test, meniscocapsular gap, and suspected 
meniscotibial discontinuity. Arthroscopic findings were used exclusively to 
establish the reference-standard diagnosis and were not entered into the 
diagnostic model. A penalized logistic regression model with least absolute 
shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selection was used to identify 
independent predictors and construct the Hypermobile Meniscus Index (HMI). 
Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling, and robustness was 
assessed with Monte Carlo simulation.
RESULTS: HLM was confirmed arthroscopically in 47% of patients. The final model 
included five independent predictors and demonstrated excellent discriminative 
performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 
(AUC) of 0.84 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83-0.95). At the optimal cut-off 
(≥5 points), sensitivity was 81%, specificity 79.2%, positive predictive value 
77.6%, and negative predictive value 82.4%. Calibration analysis showed good 
agreement between predicted and observed probabilities (calibration slope 0.94, 
intercept 0.03; and Brier score 0.13). Bootstrap validation yielded an 
optimism-corrected AUC of 0.82. Monte Carlo simulation confirmed stability of 
model performance across varying prevalence scenarios, with consistent 
sensitivity and specificity ranges.
CONCLUSION: A diagnostic model combining clinical and MRI findings demonstrated 
internally validated performance for identifying HLM as defined by dynamic 
arthroscopy. The HMI provides a structured framework to improve preoperative 
recognition and guide targeted arthroscopic assessment in patients with 
mechanical lateral compartment symptoms and inconclusive imaging. External 
validation is required prior to routine clinical implementation.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Reliability and validity of the My Jump Lab app for assessing vertical jump performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Castro DBB, Santana GAM, Carvalho JGB, Bezerra MA, Almeida GPL
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 22;64:104658. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104658. Online ahead of 
print.

Reliability and validity of the My Jump Lab app for assessing vertical jump 
performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Castro DBB(1), Santana GAM(2), Carvalho JGB(2), Bezerra MA(1), Almeida GPL(3).



BACKGROUND: To evaluate the test-retest reliability and validity of My Jump Lab 
compared with a force platform for assessing vertical jump performance after 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR).
METHODS: A total of 102 individuals, 6-24 months post-ACLR and cleared for 
return-to-sport (RTS) testing, performed the single-leg vertical jump (SLVJ) and 
single-leg drop jump (SLDJ), assessed using My Jump Lab and a force platform. 
Jump height derived from flight time (FT) and take-off velocity (ToV), reactive 
strength index (RSI) and limb symmetry index (LSI) were analyzed. Test-retest 
reliability, inter-instrument reliability, agreement and association, diagnostic 
accuracy, and association with force-platform-derived kinetic (force at zero 
velocity, peak landing force, and concentric net impulse) variables were 
assessed.
RESULTS: My Jump Lab demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (intraclass 
correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.992-0.997; standard error of 
measurement = 0.24-0.41 cm; minimal detectable change = 0.65-1.14 cm). 
Associations with the force platform were strong to very strong for jump height 
(r = 0.786-0.987), RSI (r = 0.975), and LSI (r = 0.760-0.983). Inter-instrument 
reliability was excellent for FT and RSI (ICC = 0.974-0.983) and fair for ToV 
(ICC = 0.750). Bland-Altman analyses showed mean biases ranging from -1.21 to 
-0.08 cm for jump height and -0.29 cm/s for RSI. Accuracy for LSI ≥ 90% ranged 
from 87.3% to 94.1%. SLVJ jump height showed moderate-to-good associations with 
force-platform-derived kinetic (r = 0.534-0.678).
CONCLUSIONS: My Jump Lab provides reliable and valid measures of vertical jump 
performance post-ACLR and may complement RTS assessment when force platforms are 
unavailable.

title: The Role of Systemic Antifibrotic Agents on Patient and Surgical Outcomes After Joint Surgery: A Systematic Review.
authors: Nagesh N, Romero-Padron MA, Fonte EL, Kossoff NR, Everhart JS
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 22. doi: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01368. Online
ahead  of print.

The Role of Systemic Antifibrotic Agents on Patient and Surgical Outcomes After 
Joint Surgery: A Systematic Review.

Nagesh N(1), Romero-Padron MA, Fonte EL, Kossoff NR, Everhart JS.



Postoperative arthrofibrosis (PTAF) is a debilitating complication of 
orthopaedic surgery, causing pain, stiffness, and reduced quality of life. 
Antifibrotic agents (statins, angiotensin receptor blockers [ARBs], and 
angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors [ACEIs]) have been proposed to mitigate 
PTAF, yet no systematic review has evaluated all three across major orthopaedic 
surgeries. This review synthesizes evidence on their use for preventing PTAF 
after shoulder, knee, and hip surgery. PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus were 
searched for clinical studies evaluating statins, ARBs, or ACEIs for PTAF 
outcomes with ≥90-day follow-up. Quality was assessed using MINORS and ROBINS-I. 
Fourteen observational studies met (12 retrospective cohort and 2 case-control) 
inclusion. Most studies investigated ARBs (12 studies), with fewer studies 
investigating ACEIs (7) and statins (5). The mean MINORS score was 17.6, and 
most (10/14) had serious risk of bias. In total knee arthroplasty (TKA), three 
studies linked ARBs to reduced manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) or lysis of 
adhesions, although four found no effect on MUA, range of motion (ROM), or 
arthrofibrosis. ACEI results were inconsistent, with one study showing modestly 
reduced MUA but three others no effect; ROM findings were mixed, including one 
reporting worse outcomes. Statins showed no benefit, and pooled TKA/total hip 
arthroplasty data found no drug associations with MUA. In arthroscopic 
rotator-cuff repairs (ARCRs), ARBs were associated with reduced adhesive 
capsulitis and improved ROM inconsistently. ACEI use correlated with worse ROM 
and patient-reported outcomes, while statins again showed no effect. A pooled 
analysis of arthroscopic shoulder procedures reported no associations between 
ARBs or ACEIs and PTAF outcomes. Current observational data provide conflicting 
and insufficient support for using statins, ARBs, or ACEIs to prevent PTAF. 
While some studies suggest a potential benefit for ARBs in TKA and ARCR, 
findings are inconsistent. Higher quality studies are needed to better 
understand their clinical role in preventing PTAF.

Copyright © 2026 by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.

DOI: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01368
PMID: 42912048
ai_summary: There is currently insufficient and conflicting evidence to recommend the use of systemic antifibrotic drugs like statins or ACE inhibitors to prevent post-surgical stiffness (arthrofibrosis) following major joint surgeries.

title: Digital tensioning demonstrates smaller medial and larger lateral gap measurements than manual assessment in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Borim FM, Zeng C, Lording T
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 19. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70650.
Online  ahead of print.

Digital tensioning demonstrates smaller medial and larger lateral gap 
measurements than manual assessment in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.

Borim FM(1)(2)(3)(4), Zeng C(5)(6), Lording T(5)(7).



PURPOSE: With the increasing use of robotic systems in total knee arthroplasty 
(TKA), contemporary alignment strategies have increasingly relied on accurate 
intraoperative gap measurements to achieve optimal soft tissue balance. Digital 
tensioning devices offer a potentially more objective and reproducible method of 
gap measurement; however, the relationship between digital and manual gap 
measurement techniques remains unclear. This study aims to compare gap 
measurements obtained using a digital tensioning device versus manual tensioning 
with a Z-retractor, and to explore whether gap discrepancies vary in the medial 
versus lateral compartment.
METHODS: A total of 170 primary TKA cases performed using the CORI robotic 
system (serial number SN000618, software versions v2.0.1.1 or v2.0.2.0) were 
prospectively collected from April 2024 to March 2025. Primary TKA cases with 
complete digital and manual gap measurements obtained according to the study 
protocol were included; cases with incomplete data or protocol deviation were 
excluded. All procedures followed a standardised workflow in which the default 
initial implant position was planned in neutral mechanical alignment. 
Intraoperative gap measurements were first obtained using the CORI Digital 
Tensioner (using 100 N medially and 50 N laterally), followed by manual gap 
assessments using a Z-retractor technique. Gap measurements were compared across 
the analysed flexion arc.
RESULTS: A total of 152 knees were ultimately included, comprising 78 right 
(51.3%) and 74 left (48.7%) knees. Mean preoperative alignment was 3.72 ± 4.43°, 
with a mean preoperative range of motion from 6.44 ± 6.06° to 143.34 ± 7.79°. 
The digital tensioner consistently demonstrated significantly larger lateral 
gaps compared with manual tensioning, particularly in extension (0°: 2.38 mm vs. 
1.63 mm, p < 0.001). Conversely, the digital tensioner produced smaller medial 
gaps compared to manual tensioning both in extension (-0.92 mm vs. -0.00 mm) and 
at 100° of flexion (0.79 mm vs. 1.19 mm, p < 0.001). These directional 
differences were maintained across preoperative alignment and range-of-motion 
subgroups.
CONCLUSION: Gap measurements obtained using a digital tensioner consistently 
demonstrated greater lateral opening in extension and reduced medial gaps 
compared to manual assessment. The direction of these differences was maintained 
across preoperative alignment and preoperative flexion range. While digital 
tensioning may provide a more standardised approach to intraoperative gap 
assessment, surgeons should recognise technique-specific measurement differences 
when interpreting gap data for robotic-assisted TKA planning and soft-tissue 
balancing.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

title: Hip arthroscopy with comprehensive capsular closure following longitudinal outside-in capsulotomy showed improved clinical outcomes in symptomatic borderline hip dysplasia: A retrospective study with minimum 2-year follow-up.
authors: Sha S, Liu Y, Li H, Shen L, Li W, Liu W, Li H, Yin Q
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 20;21:101226. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101226. Online
ahead  of print.

Hip arthroscopy with comprehensive capsular closure following longitudinal 
outside-in capsulotomy showed improved clinical outcomes in symptomatic 
borderline hip dysplasia: A retrospective study with minimum 2-year follow-up.

Sha S(1), Liu Y(1), Li H(1), Shen L(2), Li W(2), Liu W(1), Li H(2), Yin Q(3).



PURPOSE: To introduce the comprehensive capsular closure technique following 
longitudinal outside-in capsulotomy (LOIC) and to evaluate its clinical outcomes 
in patients with symptomatic borderline hip dysplasia (BHD) at a minimum 2-year 
follow-up period.
METHODS: This retrospective study included patients (aged 18-60 years) with 
symptomatic BHD who underwent primary hip arthroscopy for labral tears using 
LOIC and the comprehensive capsular closure technique between January 2020 and 
June 2023. The comprehensive capsular closure technique includes proximal 
capsular augmentation with the indirect head of the rectus femoris, anatomical 
repair of the zona orbicularis, and mid-capsular plication. Outcomes were 
assessed using the 12-item International Hip Outcome Tool (iHOT-12), visual 
analog scale (VAS) for pain, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities 
Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Achievement rates for the minimal clinically 
important difference (MCID) and patient acceptable symptom status (PASS) were 
analyzed.
RESULTS: Thirty-six patients (36 hips) were included with a mean age of 37.5 ± 
11.0 years and a mean follow-up of 3.7 ± 1.0 years. Intraoperatively, femoral 
head cartilage degeneration was observed in 63.9% of cases, and ligamentum teres 
tears in 77.8%. The median thickness of the middle part of the anterior capsule 
was 5 mm measured under arthroscopy. Improvements in iHOT-12 (45.2 ± 7.8 vs 79.5 
± 7.0), VAS (3.7 ± 1.0 vs 1.4 ± 0.8) and WOMAC (18.3 ± 8.4 vs 9.1 ± 3.7) were 
observed from preoperative to final follow-up (all p < 0.001). MCID achievement 
rates were 100% for iHOT-12, 91.7% for VAS, and 72.2% for WOMAC. PASS 
achievement rates were 88.9% for iHOT-12, 80.6% for VAS, and 58.3% for WOMAC. No 
severe complications occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: Hip arthroscopy with comprehensive capsular closure following LOIC 
may represent a safe and effective technique for treating symptomatic BHD 
patients, with favorable clinical outcomes expected in the short- to mid-term 
follow-up.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Estimated coronal plane alignment of the knee phenotype transitions after imageless ROSA-assisted total knee arthroplasty are frequent but not significantly associated with short-term patient-reported outcomes.
authors: Kenanidis E, Grammatikopoulos D, Papadopoulos K, Mylonakis N, Maslaris A, Tsiridis E
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 23;64:104654. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104654. Online ahead of 
print.

Estimated coronal plane alignment of the knee phenotype transitions after 
imageless ROSA-assisted total knee arthroplasty are frequent but not 
significantly associated with short-term patient-reported outcomes.

Kenanidis E(1), Grammatikopoulos D(2), Papadopoulos K(3), Mylonakis N(2), 
Maslaris A(2), Tsiridis E(2).



BACKGROUND: Postoperative changes in coronal plane alignment of the knee (CPAK) 
phenotype have been reported after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). This study 
investigated whether estimated CPAK phenotype transitions, including their 
magnitude and direction, were associated with patient-reported outcome measures 
(PROMs) after imageless ROSA-assisted TKA. We hypothesised that more extensive 
phenotype transitions would be associated with worse postoperative PROMs.
METHODS: This retrospective single-surgeon study included 231 patients who 
underwent imageless ROSA-assisted TKA between January 2022 and May 2024. 
Estimated CPAK phenotypes were derived from short weight-bearing knee 
radiographs. Patients were classified by postoperative estimated CPAK transition 
status and further categorised into minor or major change groups by transition 
magnitude. Exploratory analyses evaluated row and column changes. Outcomes at 
final follow up (mean 15.7 months) included the Forgotten Joint Score (FJS), 
Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index, and Visual 
Analogue Scale.
RESULTS: Estimated CPAK phenotype transition occurred in 193/231 patients 
(83.5%); FJS was 76.8 ± 19.9 in patients with transition and 78.3 ± 16.9 without 
transition (mean difference -1.42 points, 95% confidence interval -7.19 to 4.61; 
P = 0.758). No significant PROM differences were detected according to 
transition magnitude or direction. In multivariable analysis, neither minor nor 
major change was independently associated with FJS.
CONCLUSION: Estimated CPAK phenotype transitions were frequent after imageless 
ROSA-assisted TKA, but their presence, magnitude and direction were not 
significantly associated with worse short-term PROMs. Preservation of the 
estimated preoperative CPAK phenotype may not be necessary for satisfactory 
short-term outcomes, although confirmation using direct full-length alignment 
measurements is required.

title: Tibiofemoral kinematics around heel strike associated with heel strike transient in patients after total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Inou Y, Konda S, Ishibashi T, Tamaki M, Yamazaki T, Okada S, Tomita T
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 22;64:104656. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104656. Online ahead of 
print.

Tibiofemoral kinematics around heel strike associated with heel strike transient 
in patients after total knee arthroplasty.

Inou Y(1), Konda S(2), Ishibashi T(3), Tamaki M(4), Yamazaki T(5), Okada S(4), 
Tomita T(6).



BACKGROUND: Heel strike transient (HST), an abrupt increase in vertical ground 
reaction force (vGRF) following heel strike (HS), has been reported in patients 
after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, the contribution of 
swing-to-stance tibiofemoral kinematics to HST remains unclear. This study 
examined the relationship between tibiofemoral kinematics during this transition 
and HST after TKA.
METHODS: Seventeen patients who underwent TKA were analyzed using force plate 
measurements and validated 2D/3D registration. Tibiofemoral kinematics, 
including knee flexion angle, rotation, and anteroposterior (AP) translation, 
were calculated immediately before and after HS. HST was defined when post-HS 
vGRF did not rise gradually but showed a distinct transient peak with a 
peak-to-subsequent-minimum ratio of ≥1.2.
RESULTS: Patients were classified into the HST group (n = 8) and non-HST group 
(n = 9) according to the presence of HST. Two-way analysis of variance revealed 
a significant interaction between group and gait phase for flexion angle 
(P < 0.01). Post-hoc analysis revealed a significant decrease in flexion angle 
after HS (P < 0.01) in the HST group. For lateral AP translation, a significant 
main effect of group was observed (P = 0.036). No significant group-related 
differences were found in internal/external rotation or medial AP translation.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with the non-HST group, the HST group showed a greater 
extension-directed change in flexion angle and a more anterior position of the 
lateral contact point across the before- and after-HS. These findings suggest 
that HST is associated with a distinct tibiofemoral kinematic pattern during the 
terminal swing-to-early stance transition.

title: Increased medial posterior tibial slope is associated with patellofemoral cartilage lesions: A matched-pair case-control study.
authors: Oehme S, Arteaga J, El Kayali MK, Wolf F, Bartek B, Gwinner C, Winkler T, Jung T, Milinkovic DD
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 21;21:101228. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101228. Online
ahead  of print.

Increased medial posterior tibial slope is associated with patellofemoral 
cartilage lesions: A matched-pair case-control study.

Oehme S(1), Arteaga J(2), El Kayali MK(3), Wolf F(3), Bartek B(3), Gwinner C(3), 
Winkler T(4), Jung T(3), Milinkovic DD(3).



OBJECTIVE: The medial posterior tibial slope (MPTS) is a key anatomical 
parameter influencing knee joint biomechanics and load distribution. This study 
aimed to analyze whether the MPTS is associated with cartilage lesions in 
different anatomical regions, including the medial and lateral femoral condyles, 
the trochlea, and retropatellar surface.
METHODS: Between 09/2013 and 02/2024, 501 patients with cartilage lesions of the 
knee underwent matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) at a 
single-center university hospital. After applying the eligibility criteria, 280 
patients were included. Each case was matched to controls by age and sex using a 
1:1 matching design. MPTS was measured independently by three blinded raters 
using the Dejour method, and the mean value was used for analysis. Inter-rater 
reliability was assessed via intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Subgroup 
analysis was performed according to lesion location (medial/lateral femoral 
condyle, trochlea, retropatellar) using a many-to-one matching design. Linear 
mixed-effect regression models accounting for age, sex, and the matched-set 
structure were used as the primary analyses; unpaired t-tests with Cohen's d 
effect sizes served as sensitivity analyses. Adjusted mean differences and 
model-based standardized mean differences were reported with 95% confidence 
intervals (CIs), and location-specific comparisons were adjusted for multiple 
testing.
RESULTS: The MACI group had a greater MPTS than matched controls (9.73° vs. 
8.92°; adjusted mean difference: 0.80°; 95% CI: 0.32 to 1.27; p < 0.01). 
Inter-rater reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.921). In the location-specific 
analyses, greater MPTS values were observed in patients with retropatellar 
lesions (n = 100 vs. 200; adjusted mean difference, 0.92°; 95% CI: 0.05 to 1.80; 
adjusted p = 0.03) and trochlear lesions (n = 34 vs. 68; adjusted mean 
difference, 1.60°; 95% CI: 0.11 to 3.10; adjusted p = 0.03). No statistically 
significant differences were identified for medial (n = 73 vs. 146; adjusted 
mean difference: 0.15°; 95% CI: -0.87 to 1.17; adjusted p = 0.99) or lateral 
femoral condylar lesions (n = 36 vs. 72; adjusted mean difference, 1.01°; 95% 
CI: -0.44 to 2.46; adjusted p = 0.29). The unadjusted sensitivity analyses 
yielded consistent conclusions.
CONCLUSION: An increased MPTS was associated with cartilage lesions in the 
patellofemoral compartment but not in the femoral condyles. This suggests a 
compartment-specific relationship between MPTS and cartilage lesions in the knee 
joint. However, their clinical relevance remains uncertain.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, Retrospective Matched Case-Control Study.

title: Adductor sling and anatomic femoral tunnel fixation both yield high postoperative functional scores after medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction: A retrospective multicenter study.
authors: Guiloff Krauss R, Arteaga Correa JT, Isla Villanueva J, Prado García JL, Figueroa Berríos F, Vaisman Burucker A, Calvo Rodriguez R, Figueroa Poblete D
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 20;21:101225. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101225. Online
ahead  of print.

Adductor sling and anatomic femoral tunnel fixation both yield high 
postoperative functional scores after medial patellofemoral ligament 
reconstruction: A retrospective multicenter study.

Guiloff Krauss R(1), Arteaga Correa JT(2), Isla Villanueva J(3), Prado García 
JL(4), Figueroa Berríos F(5), Vaisman Burucker A(6), Calvo Rodriguez R(7), 
Figueroa Poblete D(8).



INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Adductor sling (AS) and anatomic femoral tunnel (AFT) 
are femoral-side fixation options for medial patellofemoral ligament 
reconstruction (MPFLR), but direct comparative evidence remains limited. We 
hypothesized similar final Kujala scores and similar outcomes regarding 
redislocation, residual subjective instability, and subsequent ipsilateral knee 
surgery with both techniques.
METHODS: This retrospective multicenter comparative cohort included 84 knees in 
78 skeletally mature patients who underwent MPFLR for recurrent lateral patellar 
instability between 2017 and 2024 (19 AS and 65 AFT cases). Exclusion criteria 
included previous ipsilateral surgery and concomitant trochleoplasty, corrective 
femoral osteotomy, or tibial osteotomy other than tibial tubercle osteotomy 
(TTO). The primary outcome was the final Kujala score. An exploratory 
parsimonious regression adjusted for age, sex, follow-up duration, and TTO; 
cluster-robust standard errors accounted for bilateral knees.
RESULTS: The final Kujala score, redislocation, and residual-instability 
outcomes were available for 80 knees (18 AS and 62 AFT cases). Median follow-up 
was 35.6 months after AS and 55.6 months after AFT (p < 0.001). Concomitant TTO 
was more frequent after AFT than AS fixation (66.2% versus 31.6%; p = 0.009). 
Median Kujala scores were 91.0 and 94.0, respectively, (difference: -3.0; 95% 
confidence interval [CI]: -8.5 to 2.5; p = 0.456). Redislocation occurred in 0 
of 18 AS and 2 of 62 AFT knees (p = 1.000). Residual instability occurred in 6 
of 18 (33.3%) and 13 of 62 (21.0%) cases, respectively (risk difference: 12.4%; 
95% CI: -8.3% to 36.7%; p = 0.347). No subsequent procedures occurred after AS 
fixation; four occurred after AFT fixation, including two in the same patient 
for the same complication. In the parsimonious adjusted model, the mean 
difference for AS versus AFT was -5.31 points (95% CI: -12.61 to 1.99; p = 
0.151).
CONCLUSION: Both AS and AFT fixation yielded high postoperative functional 
scores and low redislocation rates. Neither analysis identified a clear 
between-technique difference in the final Kujala score. Patient-reported 
residual instability was more common after AS fixation, although the estimate 
was imprecise and based on a retrospective, nonstandardized assessment. 
Prospective studies with standardized indications and instability assessments 
should clarify which patient subgroups benefit from each technique.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: A Fracture Healing Odyssey: Kinematic Comparison of Unions and Nonunions in Human Lower-Extremity Long Bones Treated with Intramedullary Nailing : A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authors: Lopas LA, Jang Y, Liu Z, Slaven JE, Arnold JC, Haller JM, Marchand LS, Mau M, Kacena MA, Natoli RM
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Oct 21;108(20):1638-1644. doi:
10.2106/JBJS.25.01333.  Epub 2026 May 4.

A Fracture Healing Odyssey: Kinematic Comparison of Unions and Nonunions in 
Human Lower-Extremity Long Bones Treated with Intramedullary Nailing : A 
Retrospective Cohort Study.

Lopas LA(1), Jang Y(1), Liu Z(2), Slaven JE(2), Arnold JC(1), Haller JM(3), 
Marchand LS(3), Mau M(3), Kacena MA(1)(4)(5), Natoli RM(1)(4).



BACKGROUND: Fracture nonunion remains a major clinical challenge. Although 
radiographic scores such as RUST (Radiographic Union Score for Tibial fractures) 
and mRUST (the modified version) are widely used to assess healing, there has 
been limited investigation into their longitudinal use. This study evaluated 
whether a log-logistic statistical model of radiographic healing scores over 
time could quantify differences between fractures that healed and those that 
went on to nonunion.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort analysis added serial radiographs of 49 
femoral shaft nonunions to radiographs from previous cohorts. Tibiae and femora 
were scored with RUST and mRUST, respectively. Scores were plotted over time and 
fitted to a log-logistic curve to generate a healing ("position") equation. 
Model-derived parameters (Y inf [ultimate score], k [a curve shape parameter], 
and t half [time to half of the score change]) were compared between fractures 
that did and did not unite. Secondarily, first and second derivatives were used 
to describe the fracture healing "velocity" and "acceleration" for each group.
RESULTS: A total of 613 fractures were analyzed: 234 tibial (196 healed, 38 
nonunion) and 379 femoral (330 healed, 49 nonunion). In femoral fractures, Y inf 
, k, and t half all differed significantly (p < 0.008) between healed and 
nonunion cases. In tibial fractures, Y inf and k differed (both p < 0.008), 
whereas t half did not (p = 0.30). The first and second derivatives at the 
population level suggest early differences in healing kinematics between 
fractures that heal and those that go on to nonunion.
CONCLUSIONS: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that log-logistic modeling 
of radiographic scores can quantify differences in radiographic healing between 
femoral and tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nails that will 
go on to union versus nonunion. Differences in healing velocity and acceleration 
may emerge early, supporting the potential of the longitudinal framework for 
earlier identification of fractures at risk for nonunion.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III . See Instructions for Authors for a 
complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Evaluations of the hindfoot before and after total knee arthroplasty for patients with varus and valgus knee osteoarthritis.
authors: Iwase D, Metoki Y, Kusumoto Y, Aikawa J, Mukai M, Fukushima K, Uchida K, Inoue G, Takaso M
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 21;64:104659. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104659. Online ahead of 
print.

Evaluations of the hindfoot before and after total knee arthroplasty for 
patients with varus and valgus knee osteoarthritis.

Iwase D(1), Metoki Y(2), Kusumoto Y(3), Aikawa J(2), Mukai M(2), Fukushima K(2), 
Uchida K(2), Inoue G(2), Takaso M(2).



BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) corrects coronal knee deformity, but 
its effects on ankle and hindfoot alignment remain unclear, particularly in 
valgus knee osteoarthritis (KOA). This study evaluated changes in ankle and 
hindfoot alignment after TKA in patients with varus and valgus KOA.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 103 varus and 31 valgus knees that 
underwent primary mechanically aligned TKA. Radiographs were obtained 
preoperatively and at 6 months. Within-group changes were assessed using paired 
t-tests. Postoperative values were compared between groups using analysis of 
covariance adjusted for the corresponding preoperative value; when the 
homogeneity of regression slopes assumption was violated, change scores were 
compared using independent-samples t-tests.
RESULTS: Hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), mechanical axis percentage (%MA), tibial 
plafond inclination angle (TPIA), and heel alignment distance (HD) changed 
significantly in both groups. Knee joint line orientation (KJLO) changed only in 
the valgus group, and mechanical ankle joint axis point (MAJAP) only in the 
varus group. Talar tilt (TT) did not change significantly within either group. 
After baseline adjustment, postoperative MAJAP, TPIA, and HD differed between 
groups (all p < 0.01), whereas KJLO did not (p = 0.11). Changes in HKA, %MA, and 
TT also differed between groups (p < 0.01, p < 0.01, and p = 0.046, 
respectively).
CONCLUSION: At 6 months after mechanically aligned TKA, radiographic ankle and 
hindfoot alignment responses differed between varus and valgus KOA. Because 
ankle- and hindfoot-specific clinical outcomes and the subtalar joint were not 
assessed systematically, the clinical significance and mechanisms remain 
uncertain.

title: Prediction model-based comparison of medial stabilized and cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty: A two-phase study.
authors: Kimura Y, Takahashi T, Kubo T, Shioiri H, Takeshita K, Matsumoto T
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 22;64:104657. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104657. Online ahead of 
print.

Prediction model-based comparison of medial stabilized and cruciate-retaining 
total knee arthroplasty: A two-phase study.

Kimura Y(1), Takahashi T(2), Kubo T(3), Shioiri H(4), Takeshita K(5), Matsumoto 
T(5).



BACKGROUND: Medial stabilized (MS) inserts have been introduced to improve knee 
kinematics and mid-flexion stability in total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, 
direct comparisons between MS and cruciate-retaining (CR) designs are often 
confounded by patient-related factors.
PURPOSE: To compare postoperative knee flexion between MS and CR designs using a 
prediction model-based counterfactual framework.
METHODS: This retrospective two-phase study included patients who underwent 
primary TKA at a single institution. In Phase 1, a multivariable regression 
model was developed using 129 CR-TKA cases to predict 1-year postoperative knee 
flexion based on preoperative and intraoperative variables. Internal validation 
was performed using 10-fold cross-validation, and model performance and 
calibration were assessed using out-of-fold predictions. In Phase 2, the 
validated model was applied to MS-TKA cases to estimate the postoperative 
flexion expected under a hypothetical CR condition. Predicted CR flexion and 
observed MS flexion were compared using paired t-tests.
RESULTS: In the CR cohort (n = 129), the mean difference between predicted and 
observed postoperative flexion was 0.07° (95% confidence interval (CI), -1.5 to 
1.7°; P = 0.996). Ten-fold cross-validation demonstrated moderate predictive 
performance (R2 = 0.218, mean absolute error = 7.78°, root mean squared 
error = 9.84°). In the MS cohort (n = 24), observed postoperative flexion 
(120.0 ± 10.5°) did not differ significantly from the predicted CR flexion 
(122.5 ± 6.5°), with a mean paired difference of -2.43° (95% CI, -6.59 to 1.73°; 
P = 0.239).
CONCLUSION: The CR-based prediction model demonstrated moderate internal 
predictive performance within the study cohort. Within the limitations of this 
exploratory analysis, no statistically significant difference in postoperative 
knee flexion was detected between observed MS-TKA outcomes and the flexion 
predicted under hypothetical CR conditions. Larger externally validated studies 
with adequate statistical power are required before definitive conclusions 
regarding implant-specific differences can be drawn.

title: A mathematical model of knee joint line orientation: Independent effects of femoral and tibial coronal anatomy and limits on achieving a horizontal joint line.
authors: Beckers G, Hengartner M, Lavigne M, Kiss MO, Massé V, Vendittoli PA
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 19. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70653.
Online  ahead of print.

A mathematical model of knee joint line orientation: Independent effects of 
femoral and tibial coronal anatomy and limits on achieving a horizontal joint 
line.

Beckers G(1)(2)(3), Hengartner M(1), Lavigne M(2)(3)(4), Kiss MO(1)(2)(3)(4), 
Massé V(1)(2)(3)(4), Vendittoli PA(1)(2)(4).



PURPOSE: Natural knee joint line orientation (JLO) relative to the ground 
remains poorly understood. A JLO parallel to the floor is commonly assumed to 
favour balanced medial-lateral compartment loading, but the independent 
influence of femoral and tibial coronal anatomy on JLO during bipodal and 
single-limb stance has not been quantified. This study aimed to quantify the 
independent effects of the medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA) and lateral 
distal femoral angle (LDFA) on knee JLO relative to the ground during bipodal 
and single-limb stance using a mathematical model.
METHODS: A two-dimensional geometric model of the lower limb was developed using 
representative anthropometric parameters. MPTA and LDFA were varied 
independently across the native varus-valgus range, from neutral to 7°, in 1° 
increments, yielding 36 discrete anatomical configurations. For each 
configuration, knee JLO relative to the ground was calculated for bipodal and 
single-limb stance, along with the theoretical mediolateral centre of mass (COM) 
displacement required to achieve a horizontal JLO. The model is deterministic 
and closed-form; results are reported to 0.1° and 0.1 mm.
RESULTS: Transition from bipodal to single-limb stance reduced JLO by 2.6° 
regardless of coronal anatomy. Each 1° change in MPTA or LDFA altered JLO by 
approximately 0.5° (0.54° and 0.46° per degree, respectively), indicating 
comparable effect magnitudes for tibial and femoral anatomy. However, MPTA and 
LDFA produced distinct geometric relationships, yielding different JLOs despite 
identical hip-knee-ankle alignment. Only a limited subset of configurations 
produced a horizontal JLO without theoretical COM displacement.
CONCLUSION: Femoral and tibial coronal anatomy independently and predictably 
influence knee JLO during bipodal and single-limb stance, and overall alignment 
alone does not predict JLO. Achieving a horizontal JLO would require substantial 
COM adaptation in most configurations. Whether a horizontal JLO is 
physiologically achievable, or the primary biomechanical objective in all 
individuals, remains unknown.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V.

ai_summary: This biomechanical model shows that femoral and tibial anatomy independently influence knee alignment; achieving a perfectly horizontal joint line may not be naturally possible for most individuals without significant compensation.
